title: Latency vs Burn-Rate: hosting mix discovery - Sapphire Insights
summary: Discovery call to understand Sapphire's cost constraints and latency targets. Discussed per-token pricing, batching/kv cache levers, tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Agreed on a short pilot to benchmark latency and unit economics; Redwood to provide pricing spreadsheet and benchmark plan.
action_items: Ethan to run a 5k-request latency+cost benchmark (varied seq lengths) and share CSV by 2027-03-09
Maya to send hosted vs dedicated pricing tiers and a modeled monthly run-rate using their sample traffic by 2027-03-05
Priya to share example request distribution and token histogram (anonymized) by 2027-03-04
Liam to confirm decision committee members and procurement timeline by 2027-03-08
next_steps: Schedule 1-hour pilot kickoff (Redwood SE + Sapphire ML Ops)
Share benchmark config and expected SLOs
Redwood to provision 48-hour dedicated pilot window if requested
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Maya, AE on the platform, with Ethan who's our SE. How are you all?
[00:00:07] Liam (Customer): Good thanks, Liam here. We run the recommender and personalized search stack, most calls are below 32 tokens but we do have spikes for long context.
[00:00:20] Priya (Customer): Hi, Priya - ML Ops. The core ask is: we're seeing costs balloon as we add features. We need to understand per-token economics and if a hosted service will let us keep latency under 120ms P95.
[00:00:35] Ethan (Redwood): Got it. Quick framing: Redwood supports hosted, dedicated, and private. Each has levers: batching, prefix/KV cache, quantization options, and routing policies. The per-token price we show for hosted is a baseline; dedicated changes the unit econ because of committed capacity.
[00:00:53] Noah (Customer): From finance side, we have a monthly budget cap and want predictable spend — bursts are fine but we need a ceiling.
[00:01:02] Maya: Totally. Can you share current token volumes and the distribution? Even a histogram helps.
[00:01:10] Priya: We'll send a sample distribution. Most traffic is short—like 8 to 24 tokens—but search rerank uses 512 sometimes.
[00:01:21] Ethan: That matters a lot. Batching helps amortize GPU startup and increases throughput, but for P95 latency tight targets we often need to tune batch size and use prefix/KV cache for repeated contexts.
[00:01:33] Liam: Quick question — if we go dedicated, do we still get the same optimizer and kernel selection, or is that a separate tier?
[00:01:41] Ethan: It's the same runtime. The difference is isolation and reserved capacity; you can pin kernels/quantization profiles. Sometimes we recommend quantized variants for dedicated to reduce memory and cost, but that has small impact on quality.
[00:01:55] Priya: How accurate are the per-token estimates? We ran some back-of-envelope numbers and they're off compared to our current cloud costs.
[00:02:03] Maya: Estimates vary because of batching and cache hit rates. If you have a high prefix cache hit rate, your per-effective-token cost drops significantly. Also model choice and sequence length distribution change the numbers.
[00:02:15] Liam: Can you give a concrete example?
[00:02:18] Ethan: Sure. Example: hosted per-token list price for the 13B baseline we quoted — assume 2ms per token on our infra with batching; effective cost might be $0.0003 per token. But if you have 60% cache hit and average length is low, effective cost can be under $0.00012. Conversely, for long-context rerank without cache the cost rises.
[00:02:39] Noah: Those are big ranges. Finance needs scenarios: best, base, and worst case monthly spend.
[00:02:46] Maya: We'll model that in the spreadsheet. We'll include assumptions: token histogram, cache hit rate, batch sizes, and percent of traffic routing to hosted vs dedicated.
[00:02:56] Priya: What about latency SLOs? We need 120ms P95 for the feature.
[00:03:01] Ethan: For 120ms P95, it depends on where you run — hosted in same region will often meet that if average length small and you accept small batching windows. For guaranteed P95 we suggest Dedicated with reserved GPUs close to your region, plus KV cache pinned on the instance. Also we can set smart routing to prefer low-latency variants.
[00:03:18] Liam: How does burst capacity work for dedicated if we exceed reserved?
[00:03:21] Ethan: There's burst pools — you can configure automatic burst to hosted tiers or a shared spare pool. There's trade-offs: burst to hosted is cheaper than over-provisioning dedicated but adds some variability in latency.
[00:03:34] Priya: Security — we need SOC2 and KMS integration, plus audit logs.
[00:03:39] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II, SSO via SAML/Okta, and KMS support for private deployments. For Redwood Private (VPC), the control plane can be customer-managed and HSM/KMS integrated.
[00:03:52] Priya: Perfect. Any gotchas on data retention or log redaction?
[00:03:56] Ethan: You can control retention windows and enable token-level redaction. For Private we store minimal telemetry unless you opt in. Be aware that certain observability features require short-term retention for debugging.
[00:04:08] Liam: Competitors like X and Y claim cheaper per-token but their numbers assume full quantization and aggressive batching that might affect quality.
[00:04:17] Maya: Right, and sometimes those are self-host numbers that don't include ops overhead. We'll include an apples-to-apples sheet showing inference-only cost and normalized ops.
[00:04:27] Priya: For pilot, we'd want a 2-week window where we can run realistic traffic and compare P95 and cost. Is that doable?
[00:04:34] Ethan: Yes, we typically do a 48-hour dedicated pilot or a two-week hosted comparison. For dedicated we can open a temporary pool; for hosted we give you a test org with usage tracking.
[00:04:44] Noah: Who owns the benchmark scripts and reporting?
[00:04:47] Ethan: SEs will provide the harness; we'll run on your sample traces or you can run in your infra and share results. We'll include token-level cost breakdown and latency percentiles.
[00:04:58] Liam: We have some regulatory constraints — EU data residency for certain customers. Can Redwood route specific traffic to EU-only regions?
[00:05:05] Maya: Yes, routing policies per route can enforce region. For Private you can deploy in your VPC in the EU. We'll note data residency in the compliance doc.
[00:05:15] Priya: A couple more specifics: our rerank path is latency sensitive and happens ~12% of requests. We need to ensure that path is pinned to dedicated low-latency nodes.
[00:05:25] Ethan: You can set routing policies by route + model; rerank can be pinned to dedicated with fallback to hosted if capacity constrained. That fallback behavior is configurable — e.g., fail-open with degraded QPS or route to faster smaller context models.
[00:05:39] Liam: What's the overhead of prefix/KV caching in terms of memory per model?
[00:05:44] Ethan: Rough numbers: KV cache can add tens to hundreds of MB depending on sequence length; for multi-tenant hosts we size for average. On dedicated you can allocate more memory and pin caches to GPUs for higher hit rates.
[00:05:59] Priya: Any real-world example of cost delta when adding cache?
[00:06:03] Ethan: We had a customer where cache cut effective token spend by ~45% for a chat-heavy workload. It depends on repetitiveness.
[00:06:10] Maya: Ok, let's talk deliverables. We'll provide: pricing spreadsheet, pilot plan and benchmark harness, and a short security pack.
[00:06:19] Priya: For the pricing model, can you show hosted as pay-as-you-go, dedicated as committed monthly with a break-even point?
[00:06:25] Maya: Yes — we'll model commit levels and show break-even weeks/months. Also show a blended strategy: route 90% of traffic to hosted, pin 10% rerank to dedicated.
[00:06:35] Noah: From finance, we'd like to see a worst-case scenario with 30% higher traffic than forecast.
[00:06:39] Maya: We'll include a stress case.
[00:06:42] Liam: On the procurement timeline — we want to move fast but need legal/security review. What's typical lead time for Private?
[00:06:49] Maya: Private deployments usually take 6-8 weeks once contracts are signed and infra is validated; hosted or dedicated pilots are much faster, 1-2 weeks for provisioning.
[00:07:00] Priya: Can dedicated mitigate the quality hit from quantization? We can't accept more than a 1% drop in model F1 for critical signals.
[00:07:07] Ethan: Quantization often has <1% delta for many families at INT4/INT8 depending on the model. We'll run evals with your test set during the pilot.
[00:07:17] Liam: If we see quality regressions, can we fall back to a non-quantized hosted variant programmatically?
[00:07:22] Ethan: Yes — routing policies and model variants make that straightforward; fallback to a full-precision hosted model is supported though at higher unit cost.
[00:07:31] Priya: A random transcription note — sometimes the tool records 'KV cash' instead of 'KV cache' — just in case the doc looks odd.
[00:07:36] (laughter)
[00:07:37] Maya: Good note.
[00:07:39] Liam: Alright, recap?
[00:07:41] Maya: Recap: Redwood to share pricing sheet and pilot plan; SE to run benchmark using Priya's histogram once provided; Sapphire to confirm stakeholders and provide token distribution. Action owners and due dates on the sheet.
[00:07:55] Priya: Sounds good. We'll aim to send the distribution tomorrow.
[00:07:58] Noah: Finance will look at the spreadsheet and propose budget bands.
[00:08:01] Maya: Perfect. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot kickoff and send the security pack. Thanks everyone.
[00:08:07] Liam: Thanks, bye.
[00:08:09] (call ends)

Note: Transcript has occasional mis-attributions and imperfect ASR artifacts (Redwood vs Red wood, KV cash/cache, SAML/SAMEL, etc.).
